newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Botswana c.bank calls for scrapping of fx controls.
newsitem.headline: Botswana c.bank calls for scrapping of fx controls.

text.p: Botswana has little to lose and much to gain by immediately removing remaining exchange controls, the Bank of Botswana says in its annual economic review for 1996.
"If the process is delayed too long it is likely that Botswana will be left behind by the liberalisation process taking place in other African countries, notably South Africa," the Bank said.

Botswana would then face the choice of liberalising in a hurry to keep up with South Africa or falling behind in the process and being disadvantaged from the point of view of attracting foreign investment.

"Capital outflows of over one million pula remain restricted, and this constrains the efficient operation of large companies," the Bank said. "Exchange control regulations constrain the development of the financial sector."

The expansion of this sector was essential to the government's policy of diversification of the economy away from its reliance on diamonds and to create significant employment for the 20-25 percent of working age Batswana in the formal sector who were out of work.

"The economy of Botswana is not very diversified: diamond mining, accounts for a 33 percent of Gross Domestic Product, 66 percent of export earnings and 48 percent of government revenues," the Bank pointed out.

"Further piecemeal liberalisation draws attention to the fact that Botswana still has exchange controls, and may therefore do more harm than good to Botswana's image as an investment location," the Bank concluded.
Recent exchange control liberalisations had not led to significant capital outflows, despite Botswana's real interest rates being significantly below those in South Africa.
Presenting a strong argument for liberalisation, the Bank forecasts that the maximum expected movement of capital would not deplete Botswana's 18,000 million pula reserves by more than 10 percent.
